meta.title: Infant Sleep & Nap Citation Tiers
meta.description: Tiered, credentialed citation data for an infant wake-windows app. Tier 1 = evidence-based (consensus guidelines + peer-reviewed norms). Tier 2 = practice-based heuristic (consultant/parenting frameworks not validated by trials). Tier 3 = practitioner convention (plausible mechanism, no direct study of the specific protocol).
meta.disclaimer: Informational only, not medical advice. Infant sleep needs vary widely; families should consult their pediatrician.

1.label: Evidence-based
1.description: Backed by expert consensus statements and/or peer-reviewed normative data. Reliable population ranges — though still ranges with wide normal variation, not targets every baby must hit.
1.appliesTo: Total sleep per 24h, broad nap-count trajectories, sleep-consolidation and circadian-development timelines, safe-sleep practices.

2.label: Practice-based heuristic
2.description: Sleep-consultant and parenting frameworks. NOT validated by any randomized trial, cohort study, or systematic review — the term 'wake window' does not appear in the pediatric sleep-medicine literature. Useful as a flexible starting estimate, not a prescription. The underlying biology (sleep pressure + circadian rhythm) is real; the specific durations are convention.
2.appliesTo: Specific wake-window durations by age; specific sample nap schedules.

3.label: Practitioner convention
3.description: A widespread sleep-consultant convention with a plausible mechanism but no direct study of the specific protocol — e.g. the ~15 min/day gradual schedule shift used for daylight-saving changes, or the standard cause-and-fix patterns for early rising, short naps, false starts, and split nights. A reasonable, gentle default; not a validated prescription, and never a diagnosis.
3.appliesTo: Daylight-saving and time-zone shift plans; troubleshooter answers (likely causes and range-based fixes for early rising, short naps, and night wakings).

sources.authors: Paruthi S, Brooks LJ, D'Ambrosio C, et al.
sources.credentials: Shalini Paruthi, MD — board-certified pediatric sleep physician; Adjunct Professor at Saint Louis University; co-director of the SLUCare Sleep Medicine program; past chair of the AASM pediatric consensus panel.
sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
sources.summary: Modified RAND consensus (864 articles). Infants 4–12 mo: 12–16 h/24h incl. naps; 1–2 yr: 11–14 h. Deliberately issues no figure under 4 months. Endorsed by the AAP. The clinical anchor for total-sleep targets.

sources.authors: Hirshkowitz M, Whiton K, Albert SM, et al.
sources.credentials: Max Hirshkowitz, PhD — sleep researcher; Emeritus faculty, Baylor College of Medicine; past chair of the National Sleep Foundation's scientific advisory council and of the expert panel that produced these recommendations.
sources.title: National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary
sources.summary: 18-member expert panel, RAND/UCLA method. Newborns (0–3 mo) 14–17 h; infants (4–11 mo) 12–15 h; toddlers (1–2 yr) 11–14 h. Note the 12–15 h infant figure differs slightly from AASM's 12–16 h.

sources.credentials: Institutional — WHO Guideline Development Group on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5; a multinational panel of pediatric and public-health experts. Authority is the UN health agency.
sources.title: Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age
sources.summary: 24-hour movement guidelines: 0–3 mo 14–17 h; 4–11 mo 12–16 h; 1–2 yr 11–14 h (incl. naps). Strong recommendations rated on very-low-quality evidence; largely adopts AASM/NSF ranges.

sources.credentials: Institutional — the AAP is the principal US professional body for pediatricians (~67,000 members). It formally endorsed the AASM 2016 sleep-duration figures rather than issuing its own.
sources.title: Healthy Sleep Habits: How Many Hours Does Your Child Need?
sources.summary: AAP's consumer-facing endorsement of the AASM figures: 4–12 mo 12–16 h; 1–2 yr 11–14 h, including naps.

sources.org: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Task Force on SIDS
sources.authors: Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I; AAP Task Force on SIDS & Committee on Fetus and Newborn
sources.credentials: Rachel Y. Moon, MD, FAAP — Chair of the AAP Task Force on SIDS; Harrison Distinguished Professor of Pediatrics and Chief of General Pediatrics at UVA Health Children's; internationally recognized SUID researcher (70+ papers); associate editor of Pediatrics.
sources.title: Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment
sources.summary: Current US safe-sleep policy (applies to naps AND night): back sleeping until age 1 on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface; room-share without bed-sharing ideally for the first 6 months; no soft bedding. Companion technical report (e2022057991) is the evidence base.

sources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.credentials: Institutional — US federal public-health agency; cites Hirshkowitz 2015 and Paruthi 2016 as its sources.
sources.title: About Sleep — How Much Sleep Do I Need?
sources.summary: Blends NSF + AASM: newborn 14–17 h; infant (4–12 mo) 12–16 h; toddler (1–2 yr) 11–14 h, including naps.

sources.org: Canadian Paediatric Society / Caring for Kids
sources.credentials: Institutional — the national association of pediatricians in Canada; this is its peer-reviewed parent-education content, adopting the AASM duration figures.
sources.title: Healthy sleep for your baby and child
sources.summary: Most nap-specific public guidance from a pediatric body: ~3 naps by 4 months, transitioning to 2 longer naps between 6–12 months. States 'napping helps a baby sleep better at night.' Totals follow AASM.

sources.credentials: Institutional — the UK's national health service; clinically reviewed parent guidance (reviewed Jan 2025).
sources.title: Helping your baby to sleep
sources.summary: Approximate figures incl. naps: newborn ~18 h; 6–12 mo ~15 h; after age 1 ~12–15 h; age 2 ~12–14 h. Room-share for the first 6 months.

sources.authors: Cleveland Clinic (reviewed by pediatric sleep staff)
sources.credentials: Institutional — a top-ranked US academic medical center; physician-reviewed content citing the AASM consensus.
sources.title: How Much Sleep Kids Need: Recommended Hours by Age
sources.summary: Adopts AASM: babies 4–12 mo 12–16 h; toddlers 11–14 h. Gives newborns an 11–17 h range and notes no firm standard exists under 4 months.

sources.leadAuthor: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD, CBSM, DBSM
sources.credentials: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD, CBSM, DBSM — Professor of Psychology at Saint Joseph's University; Associate Director of the Sleep Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia; one of the most-cited pediatric sleep researchers worldwide (130+ publications); chair of the Pediatric Sleep Council.
sources.title: How Much Should My Baby Nap?
sources.summary: Expert nap-number guidance: ~4 mo often 3–4 naps; either two longer naps OR several 30–45-min naps is normal; ~2 naps by 9 mo; transition to 1 nap between 12–18 mo.

sources.credentials: Institutional — Australian-Government-funded health information service under a clinical governance framework; sourced to peer-reviewed journals.
sources.title: Sleep patterns for babies
sources.summary: Concrete nap-number table: 3–6 mo 2–3 naps (up to 2 h each); 6–12 mo 2–4 h of naps; after 12 mo 1 nap of 1–2 h.

sources.authors: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
sources.leadAuthor: NICHD (adopts AAP SIDS Task Force recommendations)
sources.credentials: Institutional — US National Institutes of Health campaign (formerly 'Back to Sleep,' 1994; 'Safe to Sleep,' 2012), implementing the AAP Task Force on SIDS evidence base.
sources.title: Safe Infant Sleep — Ways to Reduce Risk
sources.summary: Back-sleeping for all naps and night; firm flat non-inclined surface; room-share (not bed-share) for at least 6 months; stop swaddling once baby can roll (~3 mo).

sources.credentials: Institutional — UK SIDS-prevention charity with a scientific committee; runs Safer Sleep Week; widely cited by NHS.
sources.title: Safer sleep for babies — overview
sources.summary: Own clear, flat, firm, separate sleep space in the parents' room for every sleep day and night until 12 months; always on the back; room temperature 16–20°C.

sources.credentials: Institutional — the Australian national authority on safe sleep (formerly SIDS & Kids); its guidelines underpin Australian government health advice.
sources.title: Six Safe Sleep Recommendations
sources.summary: Six recommendations applying to day and night sleep: back sleeping; face/head uncovered; smoke-free; safe environment; room-share 6–12 months; breastfeeding. Notes a safe sleep surface takes priority if room-sharing isn't possible for daytime naps.

sources.authors: Iglowstein I, Jenni OG, Molinari L, Largo RH
sources.leadAuthor: Oskar G. Jenni, MD (senior); Ivo Iglowstein (first)
sources.credentials: Oskar G. Jenni, MD — Professor of Developmental Pediatrics and Director of the Child Development Center, University Children's Hospital Zurich; board-certified in sleep medicine. Remo H. Largo, MD — renowned Swiss developmental pediatrician who led the Zurich Longitudinal Studies.
sources.title: Sleep Duration From Infancy to Adolescence: Reference Values and Generational Trends
sources.summary: The foundational normative dataset (493 children). Percentile curves for total/night/nap sleep by age and the wide interindividual variation — the empirical backbone of nearly every sleep-needs table.

sources.authors: Galland BC, Taylor BJ, Elder DE, Herbison P
sources.credentials: Barbara C. Galland, PhD — sleep physiologist, Department of Women's & Children's Health, University of Otago, New Zealand; leading pediatric-sleep epidemiologist.
sources.title: Normal sleep patterns in infants and children: a systematic review of observational studies
sources.summary: PRISMA systematic review deriving age-banded norms for total sleep, number of naps, nap duration, sleep latency, and night wakings — the strongest evidence base for what is developmentally 'normal,' with wide ranges.

sources.authors: Paavonen EJ, Saarenpää-Heikkilä O, et al.
sources.credentials: E. Juulia Paavonen, MD, PhD — child psychiatrist and sleep researcher, Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL) and University of Helsinki.
sources.title: Normal sleep development in infants: findings from two large birth cohorts
sources.summary: Contemporary normative percentiles at 3–24 months from thousands of infants via BISQ — modern corroboration of the older Iglowstein/Galland norms.

sources.authors: Mindell JA, Leichman ES, Composto J, Lee C, Bhullar B, Walters RM
sources.credentials: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD — Professor of Psychology, Saint Joseph's University; Associate Director, Sleep Center, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (see above).
sources.title: Development of infant and toddler sleep patterns: real-world data from a mobile application
sources.summary: 156,989 logged sleep sessions from 841 children. Shows consolidation from many short bouts in the first 3 months to ~two ~1.5-h naps + ~10.5-h night by 3–7 months — an objective-ish picture of the nap-count trajectory.

sources.credentials: Marc Weissbluth, MD — pediatrician and founder of the Sleep Disorders Center at Children's Memorial Hospital, Chicago; Professor of Clinical Pediatrics, Northwestern University; author of Healthy Sleep Habits, Happy Child.
sources.title: Naps in children: 6 months–7 years
sources.summary: Classic longitudinal cohort (n=172). Two naps/day well established by 9–12 months; consolidation to one afternoon nap by 15–24 months — direct evidence for the 2-to-1 transition window.

sources.authors: Staton S, Rankin PS, Harding M, Smith SS, Westwood E, LeBourgeois MK, Thorpe K
sources.credentials: Sally Staton, PhD — sleep and early-childhood researcher, University of Queensland / QUT; co-author Monique LeBourgeois, PhD (CU Boulder circadian scientist).
sources.title: “Many naps, one nap, none”: A systematic review and meta-analysis of napping patterns in children 0–12 years
sources.summary: The most rigorous meta-analysis of nap cessation. Fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2; ~94% by age 5. Quantifies the large variability in nap-transition timing.

sources.authors: Thorpe K, Staton S, Sawyer E, Pattinson C, Haden C, Smith S
sources.credentials: Karen Thorpe, PhD — Professor of Developmental Science, University of Queensland; expert in early-childhood sleep and education.
sources.title: Napping, development and health from 0 to 5 years: a systematic review
sources.summary: GRADE-assessed review (26 studies). Below ~age 2, naps benefit; beyond age 2, napping is associated with later night-sleep onset and reduced night sleep.

sources.authors: Henderson JMT, France KG, Owens JL, Blampied NM
sources.credentials: Jacqueline M. T. Henderson, PhD — developmental psychologist, University of Canterbury, New Zealand; researcher in infant sleep development.
sources.title: Sleeping Through the Night: The Consolidation of Self-Regulated Sleep Across the First Year of Life
sources.summary: Prospective diary + videosomnography (n=75, monthly for 12 months). The largest night-sleep consolidation gains occur between 1 and 4 months.

sources.authors: McGraw K, Hoffmann R, Harker C, Herman JH
sources.leadAuthor: Kate McGraw (with John H. Herman, PhD)
sources.credentials: John H. Herman, PhD (senior author) — sleep researcher, Thomas Jefferson University / UT Southwestern; specialist in circadian development.
sources.title: The development of circadian rhythms in a human infant
sources.summary: Intensive single-infant study (birth–6 mo). Temperature rhythm emerges within a week; wake rhythm ~day 45 (with evening melatonin onset); sleep rhythm ~day 56. Classic evidence on circadian-emergence timing.

sources.credentials: Scott A. Rivkees, MD — Professor of Pediatrics, Yale University School of Medicine; leading researcher in the development of infant circadian rhythms and neonatal photic entrainment.
sources.title: The Development of Circadian Rhythms: From Animals to Humans
sources.summary: Review of circadian-system maturation: rhythms are minimal at term birth, emerge over the first ~2–3 months as melatonin entrains to the light–dark cycle, and strengthen through ~6 months — the evidence base for weighting cues over the clock in early infancy.

sources.authors: Jenni OG, Borbély AA, Achermann P
sources.credentials: Oskar G. Jenni, MD (see above), with Alexander A. Borbély, MD — originator of the two-process model of sleep — and Peter Achermann, PhD, sleep-modeling expert, University of Zurich.
sources.title: Development of the nocturnal sleep EEG in human infants
sources.venue: Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 286(3):R528–R538
sources.summary: Foundational work on the interplay of circadian, homeostatic, and ultradian processes in infant sleep — the theoretical backbone for two-process modeling in infancy.

sources.authors: Webb L, Phillips AJK, Roberts JA, Serre T, Tarokh L
sources.leadAuthor: Lucia Webb (with Leila Tarokh, PhD, senior)
sources.credentials: Leila Tarokh, PhD (senior author) — Associate Professor and sleep/EEG researcher, University of Bern & Brown University; specialist in developmental sleep neurophysiology and computational modeling.
sources.title: Mapping the physiological changes in sleep regulation across infancy and young childhood
sources.summary: Fits the adult two-process model to longitudinal infant data (2–540 days). Infants build AND clear homeostatic sleep pressure faster, with a weaker early circadian rhythm — the closest the literature comes to a quantitative basis for why wake tolerance lengthens with age.

sources.credentials: Alexander A. Borbély, MD — chronobiologist, University of Zurich; originator of the two-process model and one of the most-cited figures in sleep science.
sources.title: A two process model of sleep regulation
sources.summary: The foundational framework underlying every 'wake window' idea: sleep is governed by a homeostatic sleep-pressure Process S interacting with a circadian Process C. Wake windows are a lay simplification of Process S.

sources.authors: Borbély AA, Daan S, Wirz-Justice A, Deboer T
sources.credentials: Borbély (as above) with Serge Daan, PhD (Groningen chronobiologist), Anna Wirz-Justice, PhD (Centre for Chronobiology, Basel), and Tom Deboer, PhD (Leiden).
sources.title: The two-process model of sleep regulation: a reappraisal
sources.summary: The original author's 34-year update, confirming Process S + Process C as the validated dual-control of sleep timing — the legitimate science wake-window advice loosely derives from.

sources.leadAuthor: Oskar G. Jenni, MD & Monique K. LeBourgeois, PhD
sources.credentials: Oskar G. Jenni, MD (UZH developmental pediatrics) and Monique K. LeBourgeois, PhD — Associate Professor of Integrative Physiology, University of Colorado Boulder; founder of the Sleep & Development Laboratory.
sources.title: Understanding sleep–wake behavior and sleep disorders in children: the value of a model
sources.summary: Directly maps the Borbély two-process model onto pediatric sleep — the most direct scholarly bridge between real sleep biology and 'wake window' reasoning.

sources.org: University of Colorado Boulder / University of Maryland
sources.authors: Spencer RMC, Riggins T (with LeBourgeois MK)
sources.leadAuthor: Rebecca M. C. Spencer, PhD & Tracy Riggins, PhD
sources.credentials: Rebecca M. C. Spencer, PhD — Professor of Psychological & Brain Sciences, University of Massachusetts Amherst; leading researcher on naps and memory. Tracy Riggins, PhD — Professor of Psychology, University of Maryland (memory development).
sources.title: Contributions of memory and brain development to the bioregulation of naps and nap transitions in early childhood
sources.summary: Hypothesis paper: nap transitions are driven by hippocampal/memory-network maturation (not a fixed clock). Slower homeostatic sleep-pressure buildup as memory networks mature lets children stay awake longer / drop naps — the most direct account of why wake tolerance increases with age.

sources.authors: Akacem LD, Simpkin CT, Carskadon MA, Wright KP Jr, Jenni OG, Achermann P, LeBourgeois MK
sources.leadAuthor: Lameese D. Akacem, PhD & Monique K. LeBourgeois, PhD
sources.credentials: Monique K. LeBourgeois, PhD (CU Boulder circadian scientist, see above); Mary A. Carskadon, PhD (Professor of Psychiatry, Brown, foundational pediatric circadian researcher); Kenneth P. Wright Jr., PhD (Director, Sleep & Chronobiology Lab, CU Boulder).
sources.title: The timing of the circadian clock and sleep differ between napping and non-napping toddlers
sources.summary: In-home salivary melatonin (DLMO) study: napping toddlers had melatonin onset ~38 min later, bedtimes ~43 min later, and ~69 min shorter night sleep. Shows the nap/circadian interaction that fixed wake-window schedules cannot capture.

sources.authors: Seehagen S, Konrad C, Herbert JS, Schneider S
sources.credentials: Sabine Seehagen, PhD — developmental psychologist, Ruhr University Bochum; expert in infant memory and sleep.
sources.title: Timely sleep facilitates declarative memory consolidation in infants
sources.summary: A nap (≥30 min) within 4 hours of learning enabled 6- and 12-month-olds to retain memories — demonstrating infants depend on naps for forming long-term memories (functional rationale for naps).

sources.credentials: Avi Sadeh, PhD (1958–2018) — a founding figure of pediatric sleep science; Professor and Director, Laboratory for Children's Sleep and Arousal Disorders, Tel Aviv University; pioneer of actigraphy validation in children.
sources.title: A brief screening questionnaire for infant sleep problems: validation and findings for an Internet sample
sources.summary: The original Brief Infant Sleep Questionnaire (BISQ), validated against actigraphy — the dominant infant-sleep measurement instrument used in most normative studies.

sources.credentials: Anat Scher, PhD — developmental psychologist, University of Haifa; long-standing infant-sleep and actigraphy researcher.
sources.title: Sleep as a mirror of developmental transitions in infancy: the case of crawling
sources.venue: Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development 80(1):70–88
sources.summary: Actigraphy in 28 infants (5–11 mo): the onset of crawling was linked to a transient rise in night-waking — the closest empirical basis for the popular '8-month sleep regression' (which has no formal evidence base of its own).

sources.authors: Lucchini M, Kahn M, Ordway M, Bailes LG, et al.
sources.credentials: Maristella Lucchini, PhD — Senior Clinical Researcher at Nanit Lab (formerly Columbia University); expert in objective infant-sleep measurement and big-data analytics.
sources.title: Variability of bedtime in infancy and its relationship to parent-reported and auto-videosomnography sleep metrics
sources.summary: 837 infants with 2 weeks of objective auto-videosomnography: higher bedtime variability tracked with shorter night sleep and more bedtime difficulty — supports consistent timing over rigid clock rules. Represents the emerging objective-measurement paradigm.

sources.authors: Mindell JA, Gould RA, Tikotzky L, Leichman ES, Walters RM
sources.credentials: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD (see above).
sources.title: Norm-referenced scoring system for the Brief Infant Sleep Questionnaire – Revised (BISQ-R)
sources.summary: Normalized BISQ-R scoring from 21,926 caregivers (infants/toddlers 3–25 mo), enabling age- and culture-adjusted benchmarking of infant sleep.

sources.org: INFANT Research Centre, University College Cork
sources.authors: Lenehan SM, Fogarty L, O'Connor C, Mathieson S, Boylan GB
sources.leadAuthor: Sonia M. Lenehan (with Geraldine Boylan, PhD, senior)
sources.credentials: Geraldine Boylan, PhD (senior author) — Professor of Neonatal Physiology and Director of the INFANT Research Centre, University College Cork.
sources.title: The architecture of early childhood sleep over the first two years
sources.summary: PRISMA review of 93 studies (~90,000 subjects) charting the shift from newborn sleep-dominant states to increasing NREM, decreasing REM, and night consolidation across the first two years.

sources.credentials: Craig Canapari, MD — board-certified pediatric sleep physician; Director of the Yale Pediatric Sleep Center; Associate Professor of Pediatrics, Yale School of Medicine.
sources.title: Wake Windows: Are They Helpful or Just More Anxiety-Inducing Parenting Advice?
sources.summary: A PubMed search for 'wake windows' returns zero references; the age-by-age numbers 'do not seem to be based on any scientific evidence.' Points to Iglowstein 2003 showing nap duration is too variable to predict from age alone.

sources.credentials: Erin Flynn-Evans, PhD, MPH — sleep scientist; formerly Harvard/Brigham & Women's Sleep Medicine; member of the AASM and Sleep Research Society; founder of Baby Sleep Science.
sources.title: The Science Behind Wake Windows and Why They Don't Matter as Much as You Think
sources.summary: Wake windows are 'oversimplified and misleading' — they fixate on acute sleep pressure while ignoring sleep debt and circadian timing; recommends a consistent, circadian-anchored bedtime instead. Notes there is no evidence linking high sleep pressure to difficulty falling asleep ('overtiredness').

sources.credentials: Helen L. Ball, PhD — Professor of Anthropology and Director, Durham Infancy & Sleep Centre, Durham University; founder of the Parent-Infant Sleep Lab and BASIS; Queen's Anniversary Prize (2018) for infant-sleep research; a leading academic authority on evolutionary infant-sleep biology.
sources.title: What is 'normal' baby sleep? How evolutionary clues, not cultural expectations, can help new parents
sources.summary: Argues fragmented night sleep and frequent waking are biologically normal and adaptive, and that rigid schedule-based advice reflects cultural ideology rather than infant physiology.

sources.credentials: Guddi Singh, MD — pediatrician; Centre for Public Policy Research, King's College London; BBC presenter. Peer-reviewed academic-pediatrician critique.
sources.title: How babies sleep: demedicalising and humanising the issue for child health professionals
sources.summary: Argues Western infant-sleep advice pathologizes normal infant night-waking and is shaped by cultural and commercial pressures rather than biology.

sources.credentials: Filip Drozd, PhD — researcher, Regional Centre for Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Eastern and Southern Norway.
sources.title: An overview of reviews for preventing and treating sleep problems in infants
sources.summary: Umbrella review of systematic reviews documenting inconsistent and limited effects of infant-sleep interventions — context showing the field's thin support, against which specific wake-window claims have zero direct trials.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies. Widely followed, but a commercial consultant, not an academic researcher.
sources.title: Wake Windows by Age
sources.summary: The de facto industry-standard wake-window table, copied across many other sites: <1 mo 35–60 min; 1–2 mo 60–90 min; 3–4 mo 75–120 min; 5–7 mo 2–3 h; 7–10 mo 2.5–3.5 h; 11–14 mo 3–4 h; 14–24 mo 4–6 h.

sources.authors: LoRe A; reviewed by Jansheski G, MD
sources.leadAuthor: Amber LoRe (medically reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP)
sources.credentials: Amber LoRe — Director of Pediatric Expertise at Huckleberry; reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP (pediatrician). A commercial sleep-app brand with a data team; cites peer-reviewed biology, not validation of its specific numbers.
sources.title: The First Year of Sleep: What to Expect
sources.summary: Wake-window chart plus sample nap schedules; recommends shifting from wake windows to a by-the-clock schedule around 6 months. Naps drop from 4–5 (newborn) to 2 by end of year 1.

sources.credentials: Kristin Barrett, MD — pediatrician, Cleveland Clinic. Clinic-authored, but explicitly framed as a practical scheduling heuristic, not a clinical rule.
sources.title: Wake Windows by Age: A Guide for Your Baby
sources.summary: A clinician-authored wake-window table that is notably WIDER than the consultant brands (e.g., 10–12 mo: 3–6 h vs consultant ~2.5–4 h) — a tell that the precise numbers are convention, not findings.

sources.credentials: Consumer health publisher with medical review; distinct from the 2015 NSF consensus paper. Publishes notably wide ranges reflecting real variability.
sources.title: Newborn Wake Windows
sources.summary: Wide wake-window ranges: 0–1 mo 0.5–1.5 h; 1–4 mo 1–3 h; 5–7 mo 1.5–4.5 h; 7–10 mo 1.5–6 h; 10–12 mo 3–7.5 h — much wider than consultant tables, a tacit acknowledgment of variability.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies. Widely followed, but a commercial consultant, not an academic researcher.
sources.title: Early Morning Wakings: Why Is My Baby Waking Up Early?
sources.summary: Names the consistently cited early-rising causes — too-late bedtime/overtiredness, too much day sleep, light in the room, hunger, and settling skills — and the convention that wake-ups before ~6:00 AM count as night.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies (see above).
sources.title: My Baby Won't Stay Asleep: Let's Talk False Start Bedtimes
sources.summary: Defines a false start as waking ~30–45 min (one sleep cycle) after bedtime and splits the causes into overtired at bedtime (too-late bedtime, too-long last window) vs. undertired (low sleep pressure), plus sleep-onset associations.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies (see above).
sources.title: Why Is My Baby Taking Short Naps?
sources.summary: Short-nap troubleshooting by cause: wake windows too long or too short, sleep-onset associations, and environment. Waking upset mid-nap reads as overtired; waking cheerful after one cycle reads as undertired.

sources.leadAuthor: Huckleberry (reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP)
sources.credentials: Huckleberry's pediatric-expertise team, medically reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP (pediatrician). A commercial sleep-app brand; cites peer-reviewed biology, not validation of its specific advice.
sources.title: Catnapping Baby: What It Means, Why It Happens and How to Help
sources.summary: Newborn catnaps are normal; daytime consolidation begins ~12–16 weeks; chronic catnapping often resolves ~5–6 months as babies learn to link cycles. Levers: age-appropriate timing and independent settling practice.

sources.leadAuthor: Huckleberry (reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP)
sources.credentials: Huckleberry's pediatric-expertise team with pediatrician review (see above).
sources.title: 10 Hidden Reasons Your Child Keeps Waking Too Early
sources.summary: Early-rising checklist: overtiredness/sleep debt, too much day sleep, dawn light and noise, hunger, temperature (often too cold), and schedule drift — with pre-6 AM wakes treated as night.

sources.credentials: Commercial infant-sleep program (New Zealand) produced with certified sleep-consultant input; widely used, practice-based rather than research-validated.
sources.title: Up With the Larks: Tackling Early Waking
sources.summary: Early-waking fixes: earlier bedtime for overtiredness, trimmed day sleep for undertiredness, genuinely blacked-out rooms (sleep is lightest ~2–7 AM), warmth before dawn, and consistent 'still night' responses before ~6 AM.

sources.credentials: Commercial infant-sleep program (New Zealand) with certified sleep-consultant input (see above).
sources.title: Night Waking: Causes and Expectations by Age
sources.summary: Age-by-age night-waking expectations: brief cycle-end arousals are normal and near-universal in year one; frames frequent waking as development, not disorder, and flags developmental leaps and nap transitions as common disruptors.

sources.leadAuthor: Cozy Baby Sleep (certified pediatric sleep consultant)
sources.credentials: Consultancy founded by a certified pediatric sleep consultant; practice-based guidance, not research-validated.
sources.title: Split Nights: Why Your Baby Is Awake for Hours at Night
sources.summary: Defines a split night as a long, often calm wakeful block (commonly 1–3 h) mid-night driven by low sleep pressure — too much day sleep, or a night window longer than the child's night-sleep capacity — fixed by rebalancing day and night sleep.

sources.leadAuthor: Cozy Baby Sleep (certified pediatric sleep consultant)
sources.credentials: Consultancy founded by a certified pediatric sleep consultant (see above).
sources.title: Baby Waking Too Early? How to Fix 5 AM Wake-Ups
sources.summary: The 5 AM playbook: blackout darkness, treat pre-6 AM as night, an earlier bedtime when overtired, trimmed day sleep when undertired — and hold each change for at least 1–2 weeks before judging it.

sources.credentials: Erin Flynn-Evans, PhD, MPH — sleep scientist (formerly Harvard/Brigham & Women's Sleep Medicine); co-founded Baby Sleep Science with Meg Casano, BSN, MA. Scientist-led consultancy applying sleep physiology in practice.
sources.title: Interpreting Night Wakings
sources.summary: Reads night wakings through the two-process lens: when the waking happens points to the cause — early-night wakings to bedtime-timing problems, long mid-night wakefulness to low sleep pressure, pre-dawn wakings to circadian timing and light.

sources.credentials: Christine Lawler, MS, LMFT — licensed marriage and family therapist and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of The Peaceful Sleeper.
sources.title: The 45-Minute Nap Intruder
sources.summary: The one-cycle nap (~30–45 min) peaks around 4–5 months as daytime sleep reorganizes; recommends checking wake windows and allowing ~10–15 minutes of resettling practice before ending the nap. Most babies link cycles by ~6 months.

sources.credentials: Consumer health publisher with medical review; distinct from the 2015 NSF consensus paper. Reframes the '4-month regression' as a permanent maturation of sleep architecture.
sources.title: 4-Month Sleep Regression: Signs, Causes, and Coping Tips
sources.summary: Describes the 4-month change as a lasting shift to adult-like cyclical sleep with more frequent light-sleep arousals — a developmental progression, not a temporary setback. Frames night wakings as normal and expected.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal-intensive-care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies. A commercial parenting brand; practice-based guidance, not trial-validated.
sources.title: Separation Anxiety and Sleep
sources.summary: Around 8–10 months, emerging object permanence and separation anxiety, paired with new motor skills (crawling, pulling to stand), commonly disrupt sleep for a few weeks. Frames it as a developmental phase, not a problem to fix.

sources.leadAuthor: Huckleberry (reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP)
sources.credentials: Huckleberry's pediatric-expertise team, medically reviewed by Gina Jansheski, MD, FAAP (pediatrician). A commercial sleep-app brand; discusses which age-based 'regressions' have a real evidence base and which are convention.
sources.title: Sleep Regressions by Age: What They Are and What to Do
sources.summary: Notes that beyond the 4-month change, later 'regressions' at 8–10, 12, 18, and 24 months are commonly cited but weakly supported as universal events; wakings cluster around milestones, nap transitions, teething, illness, and language/motor bursts. Prefers 'progression'.

sources.authors: Huckleberry pediatric team; medically reviewed by Salem A
sources.leadAuthor: Huckleberry (reviewed by Alan Salem, MD, FAAP)
sources.credentials: Huckleberry's pediatric-expertise team, medically reviewed by Alan Salem, MD, FAAP (board-certified pediatrician). A commercial sleep-app brand; the readiness-sign checklist and the gradual-lengthening technique are consultant convention, not trial-validated.
sources.title: Nap transitions: When they occur and how to handle them
sources.summary: The practitioner nap-transition table: 4→3 naps ~4–6 mo, 3→2 ~7–9 mo (handling 2.5–3.5 h wake windows), 2→1 ~14–18 mo. Reads readiness from a cluster of signs (fighting/short/skipped naps, early waking, split nights) rather than one bad day, and fixes it by lengthening wake windows ~15 min at a time rather than dropping a nap abruptly.

sources.authors: Mindell JA, Kuhn B, Lewin DS, Meltzer LJ, Sadeh A
sources.credentials: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD — pediatric sleep psychologist; Professor of Psychology at Saint Joseph's University; Associate Director of the Sleep Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. This paper is the review commissioned by an AASM task force.
sources.title: Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children — An American Academy of Sleep Medicine review
sources.summary: AASM-commissioned systematic review of 52 treatment studies. 94% found behavioral interventions (extinction, graduated extinction, bedtime routines, parent education) efficacious; over 80% of treated children showed clinically significant improvement that was durable at 3–6 month follow-up. The evidence anchor for behavioral sleep-intervention efficacy.

sources.org: Saint Joseph's University / Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
sources.authors: Mindell JA, Telofski LS, Wiegand B, Kurtz ES
sources.credentials: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD — pediatric sleep psychologist; Professor of Psychology at Saint Joseph's University; Associate Director of the Sleep Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.
sources.title: A Nightly Bedtime Routine: Impact on Sleep in Young Children and Maternal Mood
sources.summary: Randomized trial of 405 mother–child pairs (ages 7–36 months): instituting a consistent nightly bedtime routine shortened sleep-onset latency, reduced the number and duration of night wakings, and improved maternal mood. A later multinational analysis of 10,085 children (Mindell 2015, altUrl) found the benefit dose-dependent — the more consistent the routine, and the earlier it started, the better the sleep.

sources.org: Murdoch Children's Research Institute / University of Melbourne
sources.authors: Price AMH, Wake M, Ukoumunne OC, Hiscock H
sources.credentials: Anna M. H. Price, PhD — public-health researcher, Murdoch Children's Research Institute and Department of Paediatrics, University of Melbourne. Harriet Hiscock, MD, is a paediatrician and sleep researcher at the Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne.
sources.title: Five-Year Follow-up of Harms and Benefits of Behavioral Infant Sleep Intervention: Randomized Trial
sources.summary: Five-year follow-up (326 children) of a randomized trial of behavioral sleep techniques (controlled comforting and camping out) begun in infancy. At age six there were no differences versus controls on emotional or behavioral problems, sleep, stress regulation (cortisol), the child–parent relationship, attachment, or maternal mental health. Concludes the techniques have no marked long-lasting harms or benefits and can be used with confidence.

sources.authors: Middlemiss W, Granger DA, Goldberg WA, Nathans L
sources.credentials: Wendy Middlemiss, PhD — developmental researcher, University of North Texas. Widely cited as the source of the 'sleep training spikes cortisol' concern; listed here so the claim can be weighed against its own methods.
sources.title: Asynchrony of mother–infant hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis activity following extinction of infant crying responses induced during the transition to sleep
sources.summary: The small study most often cited for 'cortisol harm.' It measured 25 infants, with no control group, no pre-intervention baseline, and only two days of data — too limited to support any claim that sleep training harms babies. Included so parents can see the actual evidence behind a widely-shared fear; it does not establish harm.

sources.authors: Mindell JA, Sadeh A, Wiegand B, How TH, Goh DYT
sources.credentials: Jodi A. Mindell, PhD — pediatric sleep psychologist; Professor of Psychology, Saint Joseph's University; Associate Director, Sleep Center, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.
sources.title: Cross-cultural differences in infant and toddler sleep
sources.summary: 29,287 families across 17 countries: bedtimes vary by ~3 hours between cultures and total sleep differs accordingly, but daytime-sleep differences are minimal — evidence that naps run on biology while night schedules are substantially cultural.

sources.credentials: Klára Horváth, PhD — developmental cognitive scientist; research conducted at the Department of Experimental Psychology, University of Oxford.
sources.title: Spotlight on daytime napping during early childhood
sources.summary: Review of nap development: daytime naps support memory consolidation and word learning in infancy, and average nap time falls from ~3.5 h/day in the first month to ~1 h/day by age two as sleep becomes monophasic.

sources.authors: Gilchrist A, Aylward BS, Laine CM, Karp H
sources.credentials: Peer-reviewed mini-scoping review; senior author Harvey Karp, MD, FAAP. All authors affiliated with Happiest Baby, Inc. — an industry affiliation worth knowing when reading it.
sources.title: Maturation of infant sleep during the first 6 months of life: a mini-scoping review
sources.summary: 35 studies (2000–2024) on 0–6-month sleep maturation. Tracks night-sleep metrics only — as of 2025 the objective literature still does not directly measure naps, daytime sleep, or wake windows.

sources.authors: Reynaud E, Malevergne L, Touchette E, Rey AE, Mazza S
sources.credentials: Eve Reynaud, PhD — sleep epidemiologist; actigraphy study of preschool-aged children (2–5 years) — adjacent-age evidence for a 0–24-month app, applied here with that caveat.
sources.title: The interplay between nap and nighttime sleep in preschool-aged children: an actigraphic study
sources.summary: In preschoolers, an hour of extra nap reduced night sleep by only ~14 minutes (clinically marginal) while raising 24-h totals, and a nap's END TIME mattered more than its length — softening hard 'always cap the nap' doctrine, at least beyond infancy.

sources.credentials: Emily Oster, PhD — economist and Professor of Economics, Brown University; author of Cribsheet; founder of ParentData, known for evidence audits of parenting advice.
sources.title: Are Newborn Wake Windows Real?
sources.summary: There is 'no data that speaks to this choice': published newborn wake-window numbers differ site to site, and windows are best treated as one workable organizing scheme among several — do what works for your family.

sources.credentials: Pamela Douglas, MBBS, PhD — general practitioner and researcher; founder of the Neuroprotective Developmental Care (Possums) programs, with peer-reviewed publications including a 2019 Sleep Health evaluation of the Possums Infant Sleep Program.
sources.title: The science behind the Possums programs (Neuroprotective Developmental Care)
sources.summary: The strongest counter-position: sleep is regulated by the circadian clock and sleep pressure, needs vary day to day for the same baby, and therefore wake-window tables, sleep-needs charts, and 'overtiredness' framing are rejected in favor of cued care and rich sensory days.

sources.credentials: Katie McPherson — parenting journalist, Romper; reported investigation quoting pediatric sleep physician Craig Canapari, MD, and sleep consultant Kylee Money.
sources.title: New Moms Live & Die By Wake Windows, But There's No Proof They Work
sources.summary: Traces the wake-window concept's origin to early-2000s sleep consulting rather than academia; Canapari: 'not really a term used in the sleep medicine field.' Consultant Kylee Money counters that the structure works for most of her clients — useful structure, unproven numbers.

sources.credentials: Mayo Clinic patient education — written and reviewed by Mayo Clinic clinical staff.
sources.title: Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips
sources.summary: Mainstream medical nap guidance: newborns need sleep again after 1–2 h awake; from ~4 months most babies take two naps (plus an optional late-day third); the morning nap commonly drops around 10–12 months — earlier than most consultant timelines; 'drowsy but awake' for settling practice.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies. Widely followed, but a commercial consultant, not an academic researcher.
sources.title: Should You Wake a Sleeping Baby?
sources.summary: The consultant nap-capping convention: cap any single nap at ~2 h on a multi-nap schedule (~3 h on one nap) and anchor the morning wake-up (by ~8:00 AM, or 12–12.5 h after bedtime) to protect feeds and night sleep.

sources.credentials: Huckleberry Labs sleep-consultant content; blog articles carry pediatrician medical review.
sources.title: How much is too much day sleep?
sources.summary: Excess daytime sleep lowers night-time sleep pressure and shows up as bedtime battles, night waking, split nights, and early mornings; suspect it when night sleep drops below ~10 hours.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies. Widely followed, but a commercial consultant, not an academic researcher.
sources.title: Contact Naps
sources.summary: Contact naps are normal and bonding-positive, not a bad habit; safety requires an awake, attentive adult. Transitioning out, when the parent wants to, works gradually: right-sized wake windows plus 1–2 practice crib naps a day — and night sleep consolidates before naps do.

sources.credentials: Kelly Bonyata, BS, IBCLC — International Board Certified Lactation Consultant; KellyMom is a long-established non-commercial breastfeeding-education resource.
sources.title: Comfort nursing and nursing to sleep
sources.summary: Nursing to sleep is biologically normal and not a fostered bad habit; falling asleep without nursing is a developmental milestone children reach when ready — a counterweight to habit-anxiety framing.

sources.credentials: Huckleberry Labs sleep-consultant content; blog articles carry pediatrician medical review.
sources.title: How to change your newborn's sleep pattern from day to night
sources.summary: Newborn day/night confusion reflects an immature circadian clock: bright, active days; dark, boring nights; and waking from naps beyond ~2 h all help it resolve, typically by ~8 weeks.

sources.credentials: Alexis Dubief — author of the book Precious Little Sleep; long-established sleep-consultant site. Practitioner convention, not research.
sources.title: The Monumental Guide to Short Naps
sources.summary: The canonical consultant playbook for short naps, including 'crib hour' — keeping baby in the crib for a full hour from nap start to practice cycle-linking. A convention with a plausible mechanism, no direct study, and mixed real-world reports.

sources.credentials: Huckleberry Labs sleep-consultant content; blog articles carry pediatrician medical review.
sources.title: Ways to support preemie sleep: Is there a preemie sleep schedule?
sources.summary: Use adjusted (corrected) age for all sleep expectations through roughly the first two years; predictable patterns emerge ~3–4 months adjusted, and consolidated nights often not until ~6–8 months adjusted. Many preemies land between adjusted and actual age — follow the baby.

sources.credentials: Huckleberry Labs sleep-consultant content; blog articles carry pediatrician medical review.
sources.title: Getting twins on a sleeping schedule
sources.summary: The twin-sync convention: keep twins on one schedule by waking the second twin within ~15–30 minutes of the first; give the sleepier twin slightly longer naps or an earlier bedtime; per AAP, each baby sleeps on their own surface.

sources.credentials: Cara Dumaplin, RN, BSN — neonatal intensive care nurse and certified pediatric sleep consultant; founder of Taking Cara Babies. Widely followed, but a commercial consultant, not an academic researcher.
sources.title: Daycare and Baby Sleep
sources.summary: Babies can run one schedule at daycare and another at home and still sleep well; compensate a low-nap day with an earlier bedtime (even ~6:00 PM). The car-nap rule: under ~30 minutes, treat it as a catnap and stretch the next window slightly; longer, count it as a real nap.

sources.org: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Visual Scoring Task Force
sources.authors: Grigg-Damberger M, Gozal D, Marcus CL, Quan SF, Rosen CL, Chervin RD, Wise M, Picchietti DL, Sheldon SH, Iber C
sources.credentials: Madeleine Grigg-Damberger, MD — Department of Neurology, University of New Mexico School of Medicine; lead author of the AASM task-force review behind the pediatric sleep-scoring rules.
sources.title: The visual scoring of sleep and arousal in infants and children
sources.summary: AASM task-force evidence review of infant sleep EEG. Sleep spindles are typically present by 2–3 months post-term, NREM can be scored as N1/N2/N3 by about 4–4.5 months, and K-complexes first appear about 5 months and are usually present by 6. The Tier-1 basis for the brain changes behind the '4-month regression'.

sources.authors: Hammad G, Schoch SF, Engelmann M, Spock Z, Kurth S, Winnebeck EC
sources.credentials: Grégory Hammad — Neurogenetics, School of Medicine and Health, Technical University of Munich; with senior author Eva C. Winnebeck (same group).
sources.title: Charting infant sleep cycle development using actigraphy: longitudinal evidence for ultradian cycle lengthening within the first year of life from 35,000 hours of sleep
sources.summary: Ankle actigraphy in 152 infants at 3, 6 and 12 months. Sleep cycles averaged about 62 minutes at 3 months and lengthened by about 10 minutes by 12 months (parents: about 81). Median sleep bouts per night fell from 5 to 2. Source for 'about an hour', not the popular '45 minutes'.

sources.authors: Kennaway DJ, Stamp GE, Goble FC
sources.credentials: David J. Kennaway, PhD — Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, University of Adelaide; long-standing melatonin and circadian-rhythm researcher.
sources.title: Development of melatonin production in infants and the impact of prematurity
sources.summary: Urinary melatonin-metabolite study of term and preterm infants. Term babies showed little day–night melatonin rhythm before about 9–12 weeks; preterm babies were roughly 9 weeks later. Timing evidence for circadian maturation in the first months.

sources.credentials: Anat Scher, PhD — developmental psychologist, University of Haifa; long-standing infant-sleep and actigraphy researcher.
sources.title: A longitudinal study of night waking in the first year
sources.summary: Longitudinal, n=118, at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Regular night waking was 46% at 3 months, 39% at 6, 58% at 9 and 55% at 12 — it fell from 3 to 6 months and rose at 9. Evidence against a population-level 4-month rise in waking.

sources.authors: Goodlin-Jones BL, Burnham MM, Gaylor EE, Anders TF
sources.credentials: Beth L. Goodlin-Jones — Department of Psychiatry, University of California, Davis; with Thomas F. Anders, MD, a pioneer of infant videosomnography.
sources.title: Night waking, sleep-wake organization, and self-soothing in the first year of life
sources.summary: Overnight video recordings of 80 infants at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Most infants woke at every age; what changed was the share who settled back to sleep alone, and about half of 12-month-olds still needed a parent. Waking itself is normal.

sources.credentials: Anat Scher, PhD — developmental psychologist, University of Haifa; long-standing infant-sleep and actigraphy researcher.
sources.title: Locomotion and nightwaking
sources.summary: Cross-sectional, n=107, 5–8 months. Babies who were already crawling had more bedtime difficulty and night waking than those not yet crawling. Cross-sectional, so it cannot show the rise is temporary — pair with scher-2015.

sources.credentials: Osnat Atun-Einy — Department of Physical Therapy, University of Haifa (infant motor development); with Anat Scher, PhD, infant-sleep researcher.
sources.title: Sleep disruption and motor development: Does pulling-to-stand impacts sleep-wake regulation?
sources.summary: Longitudinal actigraphy plus filmed motor checks, n=20, 7–12 months. Disrupted sleep lined up with pulling to stand only in babies who reached it early (by 8 months). Small study; supports a milestone-linked, not age-linked, disruption.

sources.authors: DeMasi A, Horger MN, Scher A, Berger SE
sources.credentials: Aaron DeMasi — Department of Psychology, The Graduate Center, CUNY; senior author Sarah E. Berger, PhD, infant motor-development researcher.
sources.title: Infant motor development predicts the dynamics of movement during sleep
sources.summary: Actigraphy in 78 infants around walking onset. Babies in the middle of learning to walk slept worse than expected for their age. Ties sleep changes to the walking milestone rather than to a birthday.

sources.credentials: Anat Scher, PhD — developmental psychologist, University of Haifa; long-standing infant-sleep and actigraphy researcher.
sources.title: Attachment and sleep: a study of night waking in 12-month-old infants
sources.summary: Strange Situation attachment test in 94 12-month-olds, actigraphy in 37. Night waking was common, and secure and insecure infants had similar objectively measured waking. Evidence against the idea that separation anxiety or attachment drives the '8–10 month regression'.

sources.authors: Brooker RJ, Buss KA, Lemery-Chalfant K, Aksan N, Davidson RJ, Goldsmith HH
sources.credentials: Rebecca J. Brooker — Department of Psychology, University of Wisconsin–Madison; senior author H. Hill Goldsmith, PhD, twin and temperament researcher.
sources.title: The development of stranger fear in infancy and toddlerhood: normative development, individual differences, antecedents, and outcomes
sources.summary: Twin cohort, N=1,285, 6–36 months. Stranger fear followed four distinct growth patterns rather than one shared onset age — support for 'around 8–10 months, varies by child', not a fixed date.

sources.org: NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development
sources.authors: Weinraub M, Bender RH, Friedman SL, Susman EJ, Knoke B, Bradley R, Houts R, Williams J
sources.credentials: Marsha Weinraub, PhD — Department of Psychology, Temple University; NICHD SECCYD investigator.
sources.title: Patterns of developmental change in infants' nighttime sleep awakenings from 6 through 36 months of age
sources.summary: NICHD cohort, n≈1,200, mother reports at 6, 15, 24 and 36 months. 66% woke about one night a week throughout; 34% woke nightly at 6 months and declined to about weekly by 24 months. Waking fell steadily with no bump at 12 or 18 months, and attachment was unrelated to waking.

sources.authors: Pennestri MH, Laganière C, Bouvette-Turcot AA, Pokhvisneva I, Steiner M, Meaney MJ, Gaudreau H
sources.credentials: Marie-Hélène Pennestri, PhD — Department of Educational and Counselling Psychology, McGill University; infant-sleep researcher.
sources.title: Uninterrupted Infant Sleep, Development, and Maternal Mood
sources.summary: Cohort, n=388, 6 and 12 months. 28–57% of infants did not sleep 6 or 8 hours straight, and not sleeping through was unrelated to later development or the mother's mood. Reassurance that night waking in year one is normal.

sources.org: Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study (MoBa)
sources.authors: Hysing M, Harvey AG, Torgersen L, Ystrom E, Reichborn-Kjennerud T, Sivertsen B
sources.credentials: Mari Hysing, PhD — Regional Centre for Child and Youth Mental Health and Child Welfare, Uni Research Health, Bergen, Norway.
sources.title: Trajectories and predictors of nocturnal awakenings and sleep duration in infants
sources.summary: MoBa birth cohort, n=55,831, 6 to 18 months. Night waking fell overall across the period and problems tended to persist in the same children. No population-level rise around 12 or 18 months.

sources.authors: Macknin ML, Piedmonte M, Jacobs J, Skibinski C
sources.credentials: Michael L. Macknin, MD — Department of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, Cleveland Clinic Foundation.
sources.title: Symptoms associated with infant teething: a prospective study
sources.summary: Prospective daily records, n=125, 475 tooth eruptions, 4–12 months. Wakefulness rose slightly in an 8-day window around eruption, but 'sleep disturbance' did not, and no symptom affected more than 35% of teething babies. Teething effects on sleep are small and brief.

sources.org: National Center of Neurology and Psychiatry (Japan)
sources.authors: Nakagawa M, Ohta H, Nagaoki Y, et al.
sources.credentials: Machiko Nakagawa — Department of Developmental Disorders, National Institute of Mental Health, National Center of Neurology and Psychiatry, Tokyo.
sources.title: Daytime nap controls toddlers' nighttime sleep
sources.summary: Actigraphy and diaries, n=50, about 1.5 years. Longer and later naps went with shorter night sleep and later sleep onset. Partial support for 'check the day schedule before blaming a regression' — toddlers only, and about night sleep length, not night waking.

sources.org: Université Laval / Quebec Newborn Twin Study
sources.authors: Dionne G, Touchette E, Forget-Dubois N, Petit D, Tremblay RE, Montplaisir JY, Boivin M
sources.credentials: Ginette Dionne, PhD — School of Psychology, Université Laval; Research Unit on Children's Psychosocial Maladjustment.
sources.title: Associations between sleep-wake consolidation and language development in early childhood: a longitudinal twin study
sources.summary: Twin cohort, n=1,029; sleep at 6, 18 and 30 months, language at 18, 30 and 60 months. Less consolidated sleep predicted later language delay — the opposite direction to the popular 'language burst causes the 18-month regression'.

items.note: AASM/AAP deliberately issue no figure under 4 months due to wide normal variation.
Little day/night distinction at first; circadian rhythm still emerging (wake rhythm ~6 wk, sleep rhythm ~8 wk).
Heuristic only. Medical sources give a wider 30 min–1.5 h.

items.value: Back-sleeping, firm flat surface, no soft bedding, room-share
items.note: Applies to every nap and night.

items.value: Largest night-sleep consolidation gains occur between 1 and 4 months

items.note: Medical sources go as wide as 1.5–4 h.

items.value: Crawling/motor milestones can transiently increase night-waking ('8-month regression')

items.note: Medical sources range up to 6–7.5 h.
Fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping entirely before age 2.

items.value: Beyond age 2, longer/later naps push night-sleep onset later (day and night sleep are coupled)
